papers.title: Multimodal profiling resolves the functional and spatial organization of colorectal cancer liver metastases
papers.abstract: BackgroundColorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related mortality, largely because of liver metastases (LM). Despite advances in perioperative treatment and surgery, recurrence after resection of CRC liver metastases (CRC-LM) remains common. The cellular complexity of treatment-exposed CRC-LM and the interactions among malignant, stromal, immune, vascular and liver-resident populations remain incompletely understood, limiting the identification of biological vulnerabilities associated with disease progression and recurrence. MethodsWe used single-nuclei RNA sequencing (snRNAseq) to characterize the cellular composition and transcriptional states of nine chemotherapy-treated CRC-LM specimens. Single-nucleus profiles were integrated with spatial transcriptomic and protein-based analyses to define the functional and spatial organization of the metastatic ecosystem. We further compared tumors from patients with early versus no or later relapse and investigated candidate cell-cell interactions associated with recurrence-related cellular states. ResultsSingle-nucleus profiling recovered malignant epithelial tumor cells, fibroblasts, immune cells, endothelial cells and liver resident epithelial populations across samples and revealed substantial functional heterogeneity within each compartment. Malignant epithelial cells occupied interconnected stem-like, proliferative, differentiated and invasive states, whereas stromal, immune and vascular populations exhibited distinct transcriptional programs organized within specific tissue niches. Comparative analysis identified a fibroblast subtype enriched in early-relapse metastases, which was reproducibly identified in independent LM-CRC single-cell datasets. This population showed features consistent with a role in tumor dissemination and appeared to actively shape the metastatic microenvironment. ConclusionOur study provides an integrated single-nucleus and spatial characterization of the cellular organization of chemotherapy-treated CRC-LM. It reveals functionally specialized multicellular niches and identifies a fibroblast state associated with early relapse and epithelial and endothelial plasticity.

papers.title: Phenotypic and molecular convergence of a cancer-associated pigmentation trait in Xiphophorus evelynae
papers.abstract: Cases of phenotypic convergence are common across the tree of life, and often reflect shared ecological pressures. Studying such cases can provide insights into the repeatability of evolution in nature and help uncover the degree to which similar morphological phenotypes tend to also be driven by convergent molecular mechanisms. Here, we investigate the genetic basis of a convergent phenotype in Xiphophorus, a genus of fish known to possess a wide variety of polymorphic pigmentation traits, which have been shown to play important roles in their behavioral and ecological environments. We investigate a melanic spotting polymorphism occurring in the caudal fin that we call "confetti caudal" in X. evelynae. This trait is phenotypically similar to tailspot polymorphisms in two other Xiphophorus species, diverged from X. evelynae by ~6 million generations. We characterize the developmental progression of this trait and use a genome-wide association study paired with analysis of long-read sequencing data to narrow in on a region containing a structural variant that differs between spotted and unspotted fish. Analysis of RNA sequencing data shows that xmrk, a known pigmentation gene that falls within this region, is differentially expressed. Notably, xmrk has been implicated in the development of tailspots in deeply diverged Xiphophorus species. We suggest that xmrk is responsible for confetti caudal in X. evelynae and has been repeatedly co-opted to drive tail patterns across the genus. Despite confetti caudal segregating at high frequency within X. evelynae, we detect a number of individuals in which the spotting pattern progresses into melanoma. Overall, our results highlight convergent involvement of the same gene in tailspot traits in two distantly related lineages. However, we also find that patterns of association between the tailspot pattern, xmrk, and melanoma vary between species, highlighting the complexity of convergent evolution at the molecular level, with implications for how convergent traits emerge and evolve.

papers.title: A long-lived human gastric tissue model defines regulators of lineage maturation
papers.abstract: The gastric epithelium maintains barrier function against food-borne pathogens and executes metabolic activities through specialized cell types. The niche signals and gene-regulatory networks governing gastric specification remain poorly understood, partly due to the lack of mature human in vitro models. Here we develop long-lived engineered gastric epithelia that recapitulate gland-pit topography and, upon extended culture, give rise to all known gastric epithelial lineages including rare enteroendocrine and tuft cell subtypes. We use niche and genetic perturbations on EGE to explore patterning, cell differentiation, and gene regulation in the stomach. We establish a role for Neuregulin-1 in foveolar cell maturation, discover a novel FOXI1-regulated population resembling ionocytes and generate a roadmap of gastric enteroendocrine cell differentiation. This work establishes a physiological model that provides insights into the regulation of lineage maturation and can be employed to investigate broad aspects of gastric homeostasis and disease.

papers.title: NAD(P)H-FLIM reveals spatial and temporal epithelial metabolic heterogeneity in live intestinal organoids
papers.abstract: Metabolism contributes globally to energy production at cell and tissue levels, but its cell-specific metabolic states also support tissue function and architecture. Conventionally used bulk metabolic flux assays however provide only the average readouts across cell populations, while fixed-sample and destructive spatial analysis methods result in endpoint. NAD(P)H fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) enables label-free, spatially resolved imaging of the individual cells and their responses to metabolic perturbations, directly probing dynamics of catabolic and anabolic metabolic pathways. The application of FLIM methodology to the intact living three-dimensional tissues such as stem cell-derived organoids, linking the cellular NAD(P)H dynamics to cell identity and mitochondrial function remains challenging. Here, we combined NAD(P)H-FLIM with lineage reporters, fluorescent probes and pharmacological perturbations in live mouse small intestinal organoids. Optimised acquisition and guided differentiation revealed drastic effects of the culture growth medium and crypt-villus axis on the intercellular gradient of NAD(P)H and mitochondrial polarisation. Further, guided organoids differentiation and marker-based analyses identified enterocytes as the principal population with highest NAD(P)H intensity and long lifetimes. Enterocyte-confined high NAD(P)H correlated with higher cell-specific ATP, contrasting with higher crypt/stem cell niche-associated mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) that persisted after apical efflux inhibition. Compared to the crypt-based cells, NAD(P)H in villus mitochondria-specific and high ATP enterocyte regions was also more sensitive to oligomycin, suggesting OxPhos as their main energy production mechanism. These findings indicate greater proton-gradient utilisation for ATP synthesis potentially contributing to the lower MMP in enterocytes, whereas higher ROS levels were revealed in crypt. Altogether, integrating epithelial lineage assignment with complementary detection of MMP, ROS and ATP provide better insight in interpretation of NAD(P)H-FLIM applied in a broader context of regional cell metabolic heterogeneity, supporting future epithelial dynamic metabolic studies visualizing intestinal regeneration and disease progression.

papers.title: Deciphering lung microbial EV pneumotypes in acute respiratory distress syndrome proteome wide
papers.abstract: Background. Pneumotypes hold potential predictive value for pathogenesis, outcomes, and interventions. Lung microbiome releases extracellular vesicles (EVs). However, EV-derived pneumotypes in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) have not been studied yet. Objectives. We aimed to identify pneumotypes in ARDS patients by comprehensively profiling lung microbiome-released EV proteins in bronchioalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). Methods. We extracted EVs from 106 participants (57 cases and 49 healthy controls) enrolled in the ARDSNet and SPIROMICS clinical trials and subjected to nanoparticle liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to create microbial metaproteomics. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified by Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and spectral clustering of these DEPs was utilized to reveal patterns in microbial EV protein profiles. The association between pneumotypes and the disease was assessed. Pneumotype-associated DEPs were identified using logistic regression, and their functional annotation was performed based on the eggNOG 5 database. The taxonomy of lung microbes was determined at the species-level and ranked by biomass contributions. Results. Ninety DEPs were identified in ARDS lavage samples (53 upregulated and 37 downregulated) compared with healthy controls. There were five pneumotypes, namely, P1, P2, P3, P4, and P5, identified by clustering the differentially expressed microbial EV proteins. Few pneumotype-associated DEPs were shared among these pneumotypes and mainly correlated with ARDS etiology and organ functions. The significant difference in mortality was observed in P3 and P4 subtypes. In contrast, all patients in P1 and P5 subgroups survived. Patients in P2 and P3 groups experienced a significant reduction in both of central nervous system (CNS) failure-free days and the days without organ failure compared with other subgroups. Besides, patients in P3 and P4 exhibited a higher prevalence of baseline shock and hypertension, greater use of vasopressors or inotropes within the previous 24 hours, higher positive end-expiratory pressure during ventilation, and lower body temperature and hematocrit levels. Alpha and beta diversity analyses showed significant shifts in P2 patients. The taxonomy of the top-ranked microbes exhibited different pathogens in P2, P3, and P4. Conclusions. This study, for the first time, identified five EV expression patterns of lung microbiota in the BALF of ARDS patients. These intrinsically featured EV pneumotypes in the lung are associated with mortality, etiology, lung functions, medication administration, and disease severity in ARDS patients.

papers.title: Structural basis for m2,2G27 formation and tRNA remodeling by human TRMT1L
papers.abstract: tRNAs acquire complex chemical signatures through ordered maturation pathways in which some enzymes contribute both catalytic and non-catalytic activities. Human TRMT1L installs m2,2G27 in tyrosine tRNA and has been reported to support D-loop acp3U20 formation, but the structural basis connecting these functions is unknown. Here, cryo-electron microscopy and mutagenesis show that TRMT1L is a homodimer that extensively reshapes its tRNA substrate. One protomer clamps the acceptor and T arms and supplies the catalytic pocket, while the other engages the anticodon loop. Charge reversal at these anticodon contacts abolishes methylation without disrupting the dimer, showing that engagement by one protomer is required for catalysis by the other. Cofactor binding is accompanied by reorganization of the D- and anticodon arms that draws G27 into the catalytic pocket. In a second cofactor-bound state an active-site loop (L1) that is disordered without cofactor becomes ordered near the position of the extruded base, suggesting a steric gating mechanism that controls access to the catalytic site. Thus, TRMT1L remodels its substrate rather than closing around it, a property that may explain its requirement for modifications that it does not itself catalyze.

papers.title: Human Precision-Cut Kidney Slices as a Translational Platform for Modelling Fibrotic, Inflammatory, Metabolic and Drug-Induced Kidney Injury
papers.abstract: Introduction. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is characterised by progressive fibrosis and inflammation. Preclinical models of these processes translate poorly to human CKD. Animal models are limited by species differences, while two-dimensional cultures and organoids do not reproduce the three-dimensional, multicellular environment of the human kidney. We sought to develop and characterise precision-cut human kidney slices (PCKS) as an ex-vivo platform for studying renal disease and testing therapeutics. Methods. PCKS were prepared from human donor kidneys not utilised for transplantation and cultured in a proprietary bioreactor for up to six days. Tissue integrity, fibrogenesis, inflammation, lipid handling, and drug-induced injury were assessed by histology, digital pathology, secreted protein quantification, mass spectrometry-based lipidomics, and bulk RNA sequencing, with and without pharmacological intervention. Results. PCKS retained native cortical architecture and viability throughout culture. Slices underwent spontaneous, time-dependent fibrogenesis that was enhanced by transforming growth factor beta 1, abrogated by an ALK5 inhibitor, and attenuated by nintedanib but not pirfenidone. Single-fibre digital pathology resolved treatment-dependent changes in collagen content, morphology and architecture. Proinflammatory stimuli induced stimulus-selective cytokine and chemokine secretion through NF-{kappa}B, which was suppressed by an IKK2 inhibitor. Fatty acid treatment reproduced features of fatty kidney disease, including triacylglycerol accumulation and dose-dependent inflammation, while nephrotoxic drugs produced characteristic injury detectable across multiple longitudinal readouts. Conclusions. Human PCKS maintain renal architecture and viability ex-vivo and reproduce fibrotic, inflammatory, metabolic, and toxic responses at transcriptomic, proteomic and lipidomic scales. PCKS provide a physiologically relevant, human-based platform for renal disease modeling and drug discovery.

papers.title: H19 isoform switching during neuronal differentiation reveals a distinct pluripotency-associated non-canonical transcript
papers.abstract: H19 is one of the earliest discovered and most extensively studied lncRNAs, yet most studies have focused on the canonical 2,315-nt transcript arising from the IGF2/H19 locus on chromosome 11. We examined H19 isoform usage during the pluripotency-to-neuronal transition using NGN2/ASCL1-induced neurogenesis in KOLF2.1J human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs). We show that a smaller, non-canonical isoform, variant 3, is the predominant H19 isoform in the pluripotent cells examined. This isoform lacks the large canonical promoter-derived exon 1 and contains a short, unique first exon encoded within the imprinting control region upstream of H19. Upon neuronal induction, isoform-specific RT-qPCR showed that variant 3 declined below the lower limit of reliable quantification (LLRQ) as canonical H19 and IGF2 mRNA increased. In contrast, human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells expressed canonical H19, while variant 3 remained below the LLRQ during neurogenic, osteogenic, and adipogenic differentiation. Independent FANTOM5 CAGE datasets supported transcription initiation in the predicted variant 3 promoter region in hiPSCs and human embryonic stem cells. Long-read RNA-seq identified transcripts linking the variant 3 first exon to downstream H19 exons. Public OCT4 and SOX2 ChIP-seq datasets showed recurrent peak overlap at the upstream OSM1 candidate region in pluripotent cells, with corresponding peaks absent in the differentiated datasets examined. Together, these findings support cell-state-associated regulation of the IGF2/H19 locus and identify alternative H19 isoform usage as a feature of human pluripotent cells.

papers.title: Early Corneal Host-Response Signatures Associate with Disease Severity and Etiology-Related Clinical Outcomes in Fungal Keratitis
papers.abstract: Background: To advance host-based predictive marker development for individual risk assessment in fungal keratitis (FK), we investigated corneal host-response gene-expression signatures associated with etiology-related disease course and clinical outcomes. Methods: We compared severity, healing, and visual outcomes in 1,304 patients with Fusarium spp., Aspergillus flavus, or culture-negative keratitis. Presentation-stage corneal scrapings from 70 prospective patients underwent bulk RNA sequencing stratified by etiology, severity, and outcome. Candidate signatures were independently validated by RT-qPCR in 102 patients using clinical correlations, individual cutoff-based profiling, and masked testing, followed by experimental evaluation in corneal epithelial and macrophage-like cells challenged with live fungal spores. Results: Fusarium keratitis more frequently healed with preserved vision. A. flavus and culture-negative keratitis had the highest and lowest proportions of severe and unhealed disease, respectively, despite similarly poor visual outcomes among healed patients. Transcriptomics paralleled these patterns, revealing a distinct Fusarium host response but substantial A. flavus-culture-negative concordance. A coordinated 8-gene innate-response module correlated with ulcer size and discriminated severe from non-severe disease (AUC, 0.82-0.96), while showing more robust expression in A. flavus and culture-negative than Fusarium keratitis. Higher corneal ICOSL was associated with healing, whereas increased SLC26A4/pendrin characterized non-healing and visual impairment, particularly in Fusarium keratitis. Together, these formed a 10-gene panel whose cutoff-based profiles showed concordance with severity and outcome in masked testing. Experimental evaluation revealed cell- and pathogen-specific expression patterns consistent with patient profiles. Conclusions: Presentation-stage corneal host-response profiles capture etiology-associated differences in FK severity and outcome and identify a candidate 10-gene framework for individualized risk stratification.

papers.title: Toxoplasma gondii-induced NETs are mediated by CR3 engagement and the vital non-lytic NETosis pathway
papers.abstract: Approximately one-third of the global human population harbors an infection with the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii. The immune system exploits neutrophils and one of their effector mechanisms, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), as an attempt to capture and neutralize T. gondii. NETs, composed of DNA, myeloperoxidase, citrullinated histone 3, and elastase, play a dual role in pathogen entrapment and amplification of the immune response. Traditionally, NET release was considered to result in neutrophil cell death. However, studies have identified an alternative process, vital NETosis, that allows NET formation while maintaining cell viability. Although T. gondii induces NET formation, the associated molecular mechanisms are not fully understood, and the neutrophil fate is unknown. In this study, the promyelocytic cell line HL-60 was differentiated into neutrophil-like cells (NLCs) and infected with type I (RH) or type II (PA7) T. gondii. Extracellular DNA was found in increasing concentrations over time in both type 1 and type 2 T. gondii-infected NLCs. Immunofluorescence staining for DNA and citrullinated histone 3 at 4, 6, and 16 hours post-infection confirmed NET formation by confocal microscopy. Cell viability at 16 hours post-infection was assessed by live/dead staining and extracellular ATP measurement, revealing that most NET-releasing neutrophils retained membrane integrity, consistent with vital NETosis. Additionally, immunofluorescence microscopy at 15 and 30 minutes further confirmed the fast release of nuclear DNA, a hallmark of vital NETosis. The use of opsonin-containing human serum and an anti-CD11b blocking antibody identified complement receptor 3 (CR3) as a receptor mediating T. gondii-induced vital NETosis. These findings demonstrate that T. gondii triggers vital NETosis in neutrophils through a CR3-dependent mechanism, advancing our understanding of the innate immune response to this globally prevalent parasite and laying the groundwork for future investigations into the molecular pathways that may be therapeutically targeted to support neutrophil-mediated immunity during infection.

papers.title: Strain-resolved metagenomics shows gut microbiome signatures in a case-control study of Malawian children with zoonotic schistosomiasis
papers.abstract: In 2024, Mangochi District, Malawi, we identified unexpected cases of zoonotic schistosomiasis associated with faecal egg excretion of Schistosoma haematobium, Schistosoma mattheei and hybrids thereof (S. haematobium x S. mattheei). Schistosomiasis is associated with gut microbiome alterations, but these associations remain unexplored in zoonotic schistosomiasis. Whether people with schistosomiasis are colonised with more closely related gut bacterial strains than people without schistosomiasis is also unclear. To better understand these patterns, we conducted a case-control study, using strain-resolved metagenomics to analyse faecal samples from 36 children: 12 with zoonotic schistosomiasis (S. haematobium and S. mattheei), 12 with "classic" urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium only) and 12 uninfected controls. Microbial diversity, taxonomic composition, metabolic pathways and antimicrobial resistance gene profiles did not differ significantly between groups. However, Brachyspira, particularly Brachyspira aalborgi - an organism often associated with intestinal spirochaetosis - was more abundant in children with zoonotic schistosomiasis. We found no evidence of closely related B. aalborgi strains shared between participants, suggesting that localised B. aalborgi transmission networks are unlikely to explain the enrichment. In contrast, phylogenetic profiling across 143 other bacterial species revealed greater strain similarity between the gut microbiomes of children with any type of schistosomiasis than between those of controls. Broadly, we demonstrate the scientific value of strain-resolved metagenomics for investigating linked bacterial and schistosome exposures where local water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure is inadequate. Future inclusion of livestock and environmental samples could be used to better identify where transmission pathways overlap, providing evidence to inform integrated disease surveillance and control.

papers.title: Dynamic interactions of the coronavirus PEDV nucleoprotein with its viral partner nsp3 and RNA
papers.abstract: Summary While coronavirus genome replication and transcription occur inside double-membrane vesicles (DMVs) in infected cells, nucleocapsid assembly of genomic RNA takes place at their cytoplasmic (external) face. Neosynthesized viral mRNAs (including genomic RNA) are exported from the DMV through nsp3/nsp4 pores and genomic RNAs are believed to be selected for encapsidation through an essential interaction of the nucleoprotein N with the amino-terminal domain of nsp3. Here, we describe the interaction play between the N of porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV, an alphacoronavirus) with the N-terminal domain of nsp3 and with RNAs. While N interacts with the N-terminal domain of nsp3 with a dissociation constant (KD) of about 150 nM, it binds to diverse small RNAs, displaying an affinity in the pM range for a short RNA (RNA[8mer]). This RNA and a 60-nt long RNA hairpin were both able to fully displace nsp3 complexed with N. In contrast, nsp3 was not able to dissociate RNA from N-RNA complexes. Using truncated forms of N and of the N-ter domain of nsp3, we showed that the RNA binding site does not fully overlap the nsp3 binding site on N. These results suggest that the interaction play between N, nsp3 and RNA is unidirectional, allowing to propose a mechanistical model for genome encapsidation, model in which N is first recruited by nsp3 at the cytoplasmic face of the DMV to bind to nucleotide stretches of (genomic) RNA exiting from the nsp3/nsp4 channel and concomitantly to dissociate from nsp3.

papers.title: CurveKinetix: A user-friendly application for analysis of biological time series data
papers.abstract: Of interest to many biologists is how organisms change over time: their growth, their response to a stimulus, their movement. How quickly a process starts, accelerates, slows, or changes direction, often carries critical biological information for hypothesis testing. Extraction of these parameters, however, requires computational expertise or reliance on existing software not designed for the needed analysis. We present here CurveKinetix, a graphical user interface application that helps researchers extract quantitative parameters from time series data without writing code. Users can quickly go from instrument data files to estimation of parameters using three complementary methods to visualized data customization and export. We exhibit CurveKinetix's utility in two case studies. In the first, we show expression of an operon correlates with slowing of population level growth. In the second, we enumerate viral fusion dynamics, demonstrating CurveKinetixs framework can be applied to a range of biological questions. By making flexible quantitative analysis straightforward, CurveKinetix helps experimentalists extract more information from their data and supports clearer, more rigorous interpretation of time-resolved experiments.

papers.title: Olfactory epithelium local proteomic during SARS-CoV-2 infection in hamsters
papers.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 has been extensively studied since its recent emergence. It has proven to be an excellent model of respiratory virus impact on nasal epithelium for its massive impact notably on the olfactory epithelium using the hamster animal model. We and others have previously observed that following infection, the nasal epithelium is massively infiltrated by innate immune cells followed by desquamation leading to release of cellular debris in the lumen of the nasal cavity. This impact varies spatially in the nasal cavity, the anterior part being infected early mainly in the respiratory epithelium followed by the olfactory epithelium in the posterior part. In order to better understand the impact on host cells, we decided to use laser microdissection to analyse the proteomic of restricted area of infected epithelium taking into account this spatial variation. We observed that protein levels are mostly decreased following SARS-CoV-2 infection at 2 days post-infection which contrasts with many genes having a stable expression level. Using available scRNASeq library, we could associate the variation of protein levels to the various cell types of the nasal cavity epithelium and our findings are consistent with a destruction of most epithelial cells and the infiltration of innate immune cells. Overall, our study confirms that SARS-CoV-2-host interactions lead to profound alteration of genes expression and that while most studies heavily rely on mRNA levels, it may be decorrelated to protein levels. Our approach offers an alternative to study host-virus interactions using spatially restricted proteomic.

papers.title: Calcium Signaling and Glycerol-3-Phosphate Metabolism Coordinate Extracellular Vesicle Biogenesis in Cryptococcus neoformans
papers.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly recognized as important mediators of fungal physiology and host-pathogen interactions, but the mechanisms governing their biogenesis remain poorly understood. Here, we combined time-course RNA sequencing with genome-wide genetic screening to define the regulatory network controlling EV production in the human fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. Transcriptomic analysis identified an EV-associated regulon enriched in genes involved in vesicular trafficking, cell wall remodeling, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function and ion homeostasis. Our screen further identified diverse regulators of EV production, highlighting endosomal trafficking, mitochondrial metabolism and calcium homeostasis. Cell viability was only weakly associated with EV production, arguing against cell lysis as the primary mechanism of EV release. Genetic and pharmacological analyses established calcium-dependent calcineurin signalling as a major regulator of EV production. We identified the calcineurin target Had1 as a positive regulator of EV production and demonstrate that Had1 functions as a glycerol-3-phosphate phosphatase. Loss of HAD1 caused glycerol-3-phosphate accumulation and extensive remodeling of cellular phospholipids, accompanied by a marked reduction in EV production. Together, these findings identify a calcium-calcineurin-Had1 pathway linking intracellular signalling and lipid homeostasis to fungal EV biogenesis.

papers.title: Global evolutionary and spatiotemporal transmission dynamics of human respiroviruses and orthorubulaviruses
papers.abstract: Human parainfluenza viruses (HPIVs) cause recurrent epidemics and are a major cause of hospitalization worldwide. However, the evolutionary and transmission dynamics driving HPIV persistence remain unclear. We analysed 1,161 archived samples representing four HPIV types from seven countries using genomic sequencing and Bayesian phylodynamic inference. We show that Respirovirus (HRV-1 and HRV-3) displayed greater fluctuations in genetic diversity whereas Orthorubulavirus (HOV-2 and HOV-4) showed more gradual changes. Despite comparable evolutionary rates, the four HPIV types exhibited contrasting lineage dynamics. HRV-1 showed prolonged lineage persistence, HRV-3 underwent greater lineage turnover, and HOV-2 and HOV-4 maintained fewer co-circulating lineages. Positive selection was more pronounced in respiroviruses, particularly in the phosphoprotein gene, while positively selected sites overlapped predicted hemagglutinin-neuraminidase B-cell epitopes. Phylogeographic analyses revealed repeated interregional introductions, bidirectional transmission, and regional persistence exceeding a decade for some lineages. These findings identify distinct evolutionary and transmission dynamics underlying HPIV persistence and inform the development of broadly protective vaccines and therapeutics.

papers.title: A tricomponent mRNA pertussis vaccine elicits superior protective immunity over licensed acellular pertussis vaccine against emerging antibiotic-resistant variants
papers.abstract: Pertussis remains a major global health burden and has been resurging rapidly over the past decade. The causes of pertussis re-emergence are multifactorial, including vaccine-induced pathogen evolution, antimicrobial resistance, and crucially suboptimal protective immunity elicited by the widely used acellular pertussis vaccine (aPV). In this study, we developed a tricomponent mRNA pertussis vaccine formulated with lipid nanoparticle (LNP), designated mPervax, which encodes inactive pertussis toxin subunit 1 (PTS1), truncated filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA) and pertactin (PRN). Compared to a commercialized Tetanus-diptheria-pertussis vaccine Boostrix, mPervax induced stronger and broader innate immune activation, superior antigen-specific Th1-type CD4+ T and Tfh cell responses, and robust B. pertussis-specific antibody responses with remarkably increased magnitude and functionality. In addition, mPervax conferred an efficient maternal antibody-mediated protection in offspring mice and reshaped the immune profile established by primary Boostrix immunization towards a Th1-phenotype when used as a heterologous booster. Furthermore, upon bacterial challenge, mPervax outperformed Boostrix not only against the WHO reference strain 18323, but strikingly provided effective protection against emerging antibiotic-resistant clinical isolates that are deficient in PRN and/or FHA. Collectively, these data demonstrate that the mRNA pertussis vaccine is superior to Boostrix in multiple contexts, and therefore holds promise for next-generation pertussis vaccine development.

papers.title: Elucidating and Overcoming Lignin-Mediated Growth Suppression in Anaerobic Fungi
papers.abstract: Native to the gastrointestinal tract of herbivores, anaerobic gut fungi (AGF) (Neocallimastigomycetes) have evolved highly efficient enzymatic machinery for lignocellulose degradation. While AGF are capable of degrading lignocellulose, they more readily degrade its cellulose and hemicellulose components. Lignin is the most recalcitrant component of lignocellulose that serves as both structural support and a microbial defense strategy within plants. In this study, a negative correlation between AGF growth and substrate lignin content was quantified, ranging from pure cellulose to the lignin-rich substrate eucalyptus. Based on this observation, we investigated the impact of lignin on AGF viability and concluded that lignin delayed and slowed AGF?s growth trajectory, with IC50 ranging from 10.7 ? 16.3 mg/mL, and specifically that lignin-rich substrates decreased overall growth. Meanwhile, lignin acted as an AGF deterrent, likely by preventing access to essential sugar-based polymers and lowering overall nutrient bioavailability. However, AGF growth was restored following glucose supplementation on otherwise growth-limiting woody substrates. Through experimental, sequential serial batch culture challenge, we successfully adapted one strain of AGF (Neocallimastix californiae) to grow on lignin-rich eucalyptus. This study supports the industrial valorization of lignocellulose using AGF by elucidating the relationship between the major bottleneck, lignin, on fungal growth. It also provides a strategy for optimizing fungal strains selected for growth in nutrient-deficient and lignin-rich environments.

papers.title: Spectral analysis of gene-dependency networks reveals emergent organization across scales in CAR T biology
papers.abstract: CAR T-cell infusion products are commonly characterized in terms of their cellular populations and transcriptional programs, but these descriptions do not fully capture how a product is organized as a system. We analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data from the infusion products of 163 patients across eight cohorts to investigate how system-level transcriptional organization relates to both clinical outcome and how cellular features vary together across patients. For each patient, we constructed a gene-dependency graph using mutual information between the binary detection states of each gene pair across infusion cells. To characterize each patient's network architecture, we define spectral organization, O{lambda}, a measure of the relative persistence of collective patterns of gene dependence in the network. Using hierarchical Bayesian survival models, we assessed the associations of both O{lambda} and various established cellular features with treatment outcome. Higher spectral organization was associated with a higher hazard of treatment failure in both a continuous model (hazard ratio per standard deviation, 1.45, 95% credible interval 1.07-2.19) and a smooth transition model (hazard ratio comparing the high and low regimes, 2.03, 95% credible interval 1.10-3.53). When we investigated how cellular features covary across patients, we found that correlations among both T-cell programs and cell type proportions aligned more coherently with treatment failure risk in the high O{lambda} regime compared to the low regime, revealing a systems-level pattern that helps explain the clinical relevance of spectral organization. Gene set enrichment analysis further showed that more persistent architectures were associated with inflammation and cellular interaction pathways, whereas lower spectral organization was associated with biosynthetic and genome maintenance pathways, consistent with the hypothesis that the organizational state of an infusion product reflects its capacity to reconfigure in response to CAR T treatment. Altogether, our findings identify spectral organization as a property of the infusion product as a whole that connects gene-dependency architecture within individual products to the collective variation of cellular features across patients. This framework therefore motivates studying CAR T biology from a systems perspective alongside established descriptions of cellular state.

papers.title: Subsequent Phases of Gene Expression Leading to Commitment and Differentiation in a Eukaryotic Cell
papers.abstract: Cell differentiation requires the specific control of gene expression for each cell type. However, the mechanism by which robust developmental outcomes arise from inherently noisy single-cell dynamics remains unclear. To address this question, we performed a formal analysis of longitudinal time series during the commitment and differentiation of giant single cells. We tracked how the discrete expression states of individual genes changed relative to each other. Despite marked variability in timing and trajectories from cell to cell, we identified reproducible temporal motifs and quantified the strength of temporal correlations among early- and late-regulated genes. Notably, a core gene set exhibited the same relative temporal order in establishing stable or transiently stable expression states in most cells. This suggests that a well-defined gene expression program emerges amidst apparent stochasticity. These results support a model in which induction to differentiation proceeds via a cascade of partially concurrent, discrete genetic switching events that collectively produce gradual, continuous shifts in expression at the population level. This framework reconciles apparently stochastic single-cell behavior with reliable developmental outcomes and suggests general principles for the temporal organization of gene regulation during differentiation. Furthermore, it provides analytic tools that can be broadly applied to longitudinal single-cell datasets to design temporally precise interventions in development and disease.

papers.title: A spatial transcriptomic map of subcutaneous adipose tissue aging in male mice
papers.abstract: Aging alters adipose tissue composition and function, but the spatial organization and gene expression dynamics during lifetime remain incompletely characterized. Here we profiled spatial transcriptome-wide changes in the aging male murine inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT). We describe ten different cell type clusters and three distinct adipocyte states. Further, we detected lipid-associated macrophages (LAMs), the cell type-enriched cluster with the largest number of genes upregulated in old age. LAMs that engage in local crown-like structures (CLS) are associated with pro-inflammatory niche programs at old age while LAMs outside of CLS are enriched in metabolically active transcriptional programmes at young age. LAM spots show reduced predicted lipid oxidation and glycolytic activity with age. Independent validation confirmed functionally reduced glycolytic capacity in aged female and male LAMs. Together, our study provides a deeply sequenced spatiotemporal resource for investigating adipose tissue aging biology, and for prioritizing spatially defined macrophage niches.

papers.title: Tritrophic Interactions among Crapemyrtle, Crapemyrtle Aphids, and the Green Lacewing Chrysoperla rufilabris (Burmeister)
papers.abstract: Tritrophic interactions can have considerable impact on biological control systems, therefore, it is imperative to consider these interactions when implementing or evaluating biological control agents. Crape myrtles, Lagerstroemia indica L. x L. fauriei L., are important non-native ornamental plants from Asia that are widely planted and a major woody landscape species in the southern U.S. Six alkaloids have been identified from L. indica, mostly in the seeds and leaves. Crapemyrtle aphids, Tinocallis kahawaluokalani (Kirkaldy), are host specific to crape myrtle and have been shown to be important prey for many native beneficial insects including coccinellids, mirids, and green lacewings. The crapemyrtle aphids occur in different densities per leaf on crape myrtle cultivars and some native beneficial insects cannot fully develop by feeding solely on these aphids. Moreover, no parasitoids of crapemyrtle aphids are known. This information suggests that plant chemistry is involved in tritrophic interactions between this plant, its herbivores and their natural enemies. The purpose of this study was to investigate the suitability of crapemyrtle aphids as a food source for the green lacewing Chrysoperla rufilabris (Bermeister). Experiments were conducted to test the effects of crapemyrtle cultivar, mature plant height, and source of germplasm on the life history characteristics of C. rufilabris. Crapemyrtle aphids were reared on seven cultivars of crapemyrtle, including Apalachee, Natchez, Sioux, Tuscarora, Lipan, Carolina Beauty, and Byers Wonderful White. Aphids from each cultivar were fed exclusively to green lacewing larvae from egg to adult eclosion. Survivorship by cultivar treatment was determined for developmental stages and growth parameters. Cultivar did not affect larval survival but did affect pupal and total survivorship. Length of pupation was extended by aphids feeding on mid mature height cultivars. Dry mass of larvae and adults were also affected accordingly. Males had lower dry mass than females. Lacewings fed on aphids from tall mature height cultivars developed higher dry mass.

papers.title: Multi-omics analysis reveals how the natural compound bostrycin induces iron starvation and ferroptosis
papers.abstract: The development of novel anticancer drugs remains urgent due to limited efficacy of existing therapies. Natural products are a rich source for discovery of anticancer agents, yet their mechanisms often remain elusive. Bostrycin, a fungal anthraquinone with broad cytotoxicity, is one such compound. Here, we combine global and nascent proteomics with metabolomics to elucidate the mechanism of bostrycin-induced cell death. We show that bostrycin induces ferroptosis, and use thermal proteome profiling to identify thioredoxin reductase 1 (TXNRD1), a key enzyme in glutathione metabolism and redox control, as bostrycin's primary direct target. Bostrycin triggered an iron starvation response and reduced iron-sulfur cluster-containing proteins, consistent with impaired cysteine availability. While the resulting iron overload likely triggered ferroptotic death, this coincided with broader disruption of redox balance, glutathione metabolism, and energy pathways. These findings establish bostrycin's mechanism of action and identify it as a ferroptosis-inducing agent acting distinctly from canonical inducers.

papers.title: A spatiotemporal perturbational atlas of the post-pneumonectomy lung
papers.abstract: Perturbational spatial atlases have begun to map regenerative dynamics in a variety of tissues, yet lung remodeling has not been characterized at comparable spatial and temporal resolution. Post-pneumonectomy lung regeneration (PPLR) provides a tractable mammalian model for tissue regeneration that can be studied in situ. Here, we present a spatiotemporal perturbational atlas of PPLR in Rattus norvegicus, combining single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq), high-resolution spatial transcriptomics (10x Genomics Xenium), and NICHES-based spatial tissue connectomics. We observe three distinct tissue architectures at successive timepoints after pneumonectomy, each characterized by coordinated shifts in local cellular composition and intercellular signaling. At Day 3 (D3), a line of interstitial macrophages colocalizes directly beneath an intact mesothelium among active mechanotransductive and inflammatory signaling. We also observe the unexpected appearance of a transitional remodeling cellular community at D7 which appears largely absent at later timepoints, marked by fibrosis- mimetic signaling. At D14, an alveologenic architecture at distal lung tissue displays a connectivity signature consistent with active de novo growth, distinct from baseline homeostasis. Our findings establish a spatiotemporal map of multicellular architecture during regenerative lung remodeling and introduce a generalizable framework for spatial connectomic analysis to be used in perturbational tissue systems biology.

papers.title: Natural and synthetic polyamines as organic counterions for multi-crossover DNA nanostructures
papers.abstract: Assembly of DNA nanostructures requires positive counterions to shield the negative charge repulsion between the strands in the assembly. While several counterions have been explored for DNA nanostructure assembly, polyamines are particularly attractive candidates because they could support intracellular assembly of DNA nanostructures. However, a systematic analysis of natural and synthetic polyamines for DNA nanostructure assembly is currently lacking. In this study, we demonstrate the assembly of three model DNA nanostructures of the same size but with different number and topology of crossovers using three naturally occurring and two synthetic polyamines. The model DNA nanostructures are a double crossover motif with two antiparallel crossovers (DX-A), a double crossover motif with two parallel crossovers (DX-P), and a paranemic crossover with six parallel crossovers (PX). We successfully assembled all nanostructures, and relative assembly yields depended on the concentration and the type of polyamine and the type of DNA nanostructure. The structures exhibited comparable conformations but displayed slightly lower thermal stabilities compared to their Mg2+ assembled counterparts. We also demonstrate hierarchical assembly of DX tiles into periodic 2D lattices using the polyamines. Our results shed light on how polyamines differentially impact DNA nanostructures with distinct topological features and different crossover densities. Polyamines can serve as organic biocompatible counterions for the assembly of simple DNA motifs as well as larger arrays with implications for intracellular assembly and biological applications of DNA nanostructures.

papers.title: Engineering acidophilic non-conventional yeasts as low-pH cell factories for organic acid production
papers.abstract: Acidophilic non-conventional yeasts (NCYs) thrive at low pH and are promising hosts for organic acid production, but their use is limited by the availability of genetic engineering tools. Here, we optimised a chemical transformation protocol for efficient DNA delivery into six NCYs, including M. bulderi, S. bombicola, S. batistae, K. aerobia, K. naganishii and Y. lipolytica. We also developed Pan/ARS-containing expression vectors compatible with YeastFab for one-pot assembly of standardised promoters, open reading frames and terminators. As a proof of concept, we engineered M. bulderi, S. bombicola and S. batistae to produce lactic acid. We combined codon-optimised ldh genes from B. megaterium and L. helveticus with regulatory elements from S. cerevisiae or M. bulderi and introduced the resulting constructs into the hosts on episomal vectors. Lactic acid titres varied substantially across hosts and constructs. The highest titre, approximately 6.4 g/L, was achieved in S. batistae expressing the B. megaterium ldh gene under the control of S. cerevisiae regulatory elements. For targeted genome engineering, we developed a CREEPY-derived CRISPR-Cas9 system that supports multiplex gRNA assembly and achieved over 94% gene deletion efficiency in S. bombicola. In Starmerella species, Aro10p contributes to the conversion of pyruvate to acetaldehyde, potentially diverting carbon away from lactic acid production. Deleting ARO10 in S. bombicola increased lactic acid production through both endogenous and exogenous ldh pathways, with titres reaching up to 6 g/L. S. bombicola was unable to grow on lactate as the sole carbon source, whereas S. batistae utilised both D-lactate and L-lactate. This suggests that S. bombicola may offer a production advantage by limiting lactate reassimilation. Together, these genetic tools and metabolic engineering strategies expand the engineering capabilities of acidophilic NCYs and lay the groundwork for developing these yeasts as low-pH cell factories for the sustainable production of organic acids and other bio-based chemicals.

papers.title: Engineering dynamic interkingdom communication between synthetic organelles and mammalian systems
papers.abstract: Engineering intracellular microbes to function as synthetic organelles, or quasiorganelles, opens new avenues for controlling mammalian cell fates and function through programmable and quantitative interkingdom communication. Here, we develop a bioluminescent reporter platform to quantify the magnitude, kinetics, persistence, and spatial distribution of transcriptional regulation in mammalian host cells directed by quasiorganelles. Using an attenuated, flavin-auxotrophic Listeria monocytogenes chassis (LINQ1) engineered to deliver synthetic transcription factors, we demonstrate approximately 100-fold activation of mammalian reporter genes, with distinct kinetics and dynamics for the tetracycline transactivator and Gal4 systems. In transgenic reporter mice, LINQ1 induced approximately 25-fold reporter activation across multiple organs, with activity persisting beyond three weeks in some animals. In mice bearing triple-negative breast tumors, LINQ1 activated intratumoral transcription and, incidentally, transiently suppressed tumor growth, although responses diminished with repeated administration. These findings establish a quantitative foundation for engineering interkingdom communication in vivo to advance a new paradigm in which programmable microbial systems function as synthetic organelles to direct mammalian cell fates and function for therapeutic benefit.

papers.title: Uncovering mechanisms of cell-free protein synthesis using tailored coarse-grained models
papers.abstract: Cell-free protein synthesis has revolutionised molecular biology research, and it continues to be a fundamental methodology in synthetic biology today. Yet, many of its mechanistic principles remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to predict reaction behaviour. In this work, we introduce a pipeline for uncovering these principles that combines computational models with experimental validation in a design-build-test-learn cycle. First, we develop a coarse-grained ordinary differential equation model describing key processes in the reaction. Next, we adapt the model to predict system behaviour under competing mechanistic hypotheses and compare model predictions to our experimental data from batch reactions using Escherichia coli extract. Our data and analysis indicate that gene length determines the rate-limiting step in transcription; it identifies transcription/translation-independent depletion of chemical energy as the primary cause for reaction termination; and finally it highlights translation as the most variable process between batches of cellular extract. Together, these results point to strategies for improving the yield and reproducibility of cell-free protein synthesis, and provide a framework for rational, model-guided design of cell-free systems.

papers.title: Virulence evolution of stem and stripe rust towards the widely-deployed Sr31/Yr9 wheat resistance gene combination
papers.abstract: The wheat Sr31 resistance gene encoded on the 1BL.1RS wheat-rye recombinant chromosome provided durable, broad-spectrum protection against stem rust, caused by Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici (Pgt), until the emergence of the virulent Ug99 lineage in 1998. Using mutant sequencing, we identify both the stem rust avirulence effector AvrSr31 and its cognate wheat resistance gene Sr31. The Ug99 epidemic strain arose through a single mutation of the AvrSr31-01 allele in a progenitor lineage that was heterozygous at this locus. The Sr31 paralog Yr9, also encoded on 1RS, recognizes an unrelated effector, AvrYr9, from P. striiformis f. sp. tritici (Pst), identified here via a high-throughput effector library screen. In Pst, virulence on Yr9 evolved through amino acid substitutions at two adjacent residues and expression polymorphisms that suppress AvrYr9 recognition. AvrSr31 variants in Pgt are more variable, with 22 polymorphic amino acid sites, but most variants are recognised by Sr31, except AvrSr31-03 in which two unique amino changes cause loss of recognition. These findings reveal how Pgt and Pst independently overcame two of the most widely deployed resistance genes in wheat and provide a foundation for the informed deployment of resistance against these globally important pathogens.

papers.title: Cultivar-specific transposable element insertions are associated with both suppression and dominance of homoeolog expression in bread wheat
papers.abstract: Bread wheat is an allohexaploid in which the three homoeologous copies of most genes are expressed unequally, and transposable elements (TEs) occupying gene bodies have been proposed as one source of that imbalance. Previous tests of this idea examined a single genotype, so they could not ask whether differences in insertion between cultivars correspond to differences in expression. We sequenced young-leaf transcriptomes of six bread wheat cultivars, quantified them against IWGSC RefSeq v2.1, and combined them with transposable element annotations generated independently for each cultivar's own genome. Between 29.47% and 29.64% of genes carried an element that lay entirely within the gene body, 85% of which were intronic. Across all 12,887 homoeologous groups analyzed, agreement between insertion and expression exceeded a permutation null only modestly. Restricting the test to the 1,692 groups whose insertion pattern differs between cultivars changed the picture: 115 of these showed expression bias tracking the insertion, against 27.3 expected, a 4.21-fold enrichment. The association was markedly asymmetric, reaching 6.83-fold for suppression of the inserted homoeolog but 2.53-fold for dominance, and it was carried by intronic rather than coding-sequence insertions and by six of eleven element superfamilies. The same trend was observed across all six tissues in an independently generated wheat pan-transcriptome, where quantifying the same reads against each cultivar's own genome assembly confirmed the association independently of the reference used. We identified 74 candidate loci at which polymorphic insertions were associated with consistent transcriptional suppression across all six cultivars. These findings reveal polymorphic TE insertions as a source of evolutionary variation in homoeolog expression, linking genome structural diversity to transcriptional diversification in bread wheat.
